commit.message:
Ignore the pitch diagram source alongside the rest of the pitch material

docs/pitch-diagram.mmd is the flowchart shown during the pitch. Same category
as the script, the PDF and the builder: prep material, not a deliverable.

Only the rule is committed. Nothing pitch-related is tracked.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Widen the pitch ignore rule to cover the PDF and its generator

docs/PITCH.md was already excluded. The PDF, the paste-along command file and
the builder script are the same material in other forms - and the builder is
the one that matters, because it embeds every spoken line. Committing it
would publish exactly what keeping the PDF back was meant to prevent.

Only the rule is committed. Nothing pitch-related is tracked.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Keep pitch material out of the repo

docs/PITCH.md was committed and pushed by mistake, then purged from all 25
commits with git-filter-repo and force-pushed. This adds the ignore rule so
it cannot be swept up by `git add -A` again.

It is prep material rather than a deliverable: a script telling a panel how
to answer their own questions reads badly to that panel. No credentials were
involved - the exposure was embarrassing rather than dangerous - but the
repo is read by judges and this is not for them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add the five-minute pitch script, timed against measured runtimes

The video is a hard submission requirement and was the only unstarted one.
The script is built entirely from demos that run today with no API key, no
server and no network.

Timing is measured rather than estimated: all three demos finish in about a
second. That matters for recording, because it means narration carries the
time rather than execution - paste, let the output land, talk over a static
screen. The script budgets 75 seconds over demo one, 45 over demo two, 20
over demo three, and says so.

Two structural choices worth naming.

The strongest thirty seconds is the cost sweep, where the honest answer is
that at a Rs 250 filing cost the system loses to fighting everything. Showing
the number where it loses is what makes the crossover claim mean anything,
and the script marks it as not-to-be-cut.

Limitations come near the end rather than being omitted: the LLM drafters
have never run live, extraction covers 21 of 175 documents, 17 of 20 rulebook
entries are unverified. A panel that finds those itself discounts everything
around them.

Also includes a cut list in priority order for running long, and short
answers to the five questions a payments panel is most likely to ask.

README now leads with `run` rather than `demo`, since one command showing
eight stages is a better first impression than one showing a decision.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add `vakil run` - one dispute, all eight stages, one command

Every stage had been built and tested; none had ever been run as one thing
outside an ad-hoc script. A judge could run six pieces of the system and be
told the seams held. That is a different claim from the system working.

One invocation now goes record to filing, each stage labelled code or model
so the boundary the design rests on is visible rather than asserted. It needs
no API key: the decision path is deterministic, the default drafter builds
sentences from facts, and filing goes to the bundled mock in process rather
than requiring docker compose first.

Stopping early is reported as a result with a reason rather than a failure.
Most disputes should not be filed, and a runner that treated a fold as an
error would be arguing with its own decision engine.

Running --drop delivery end to end exposed something the stage tests could
not: withdrawing the courier document shortens the letter and then makes the
filing impossible, because no documents remain to attach. Two independent
guards agreeing about the same missing evidence, neither aware of the other.
That coherence is only observable end to end.

It also surfaced a real typing bug. RazorpayClient declared httpx.Client and
every test passed, because Starlette's TestClient duck-types into it - but
TestClient subclasses httpx2.Client, a different package. The declaration was
false and mypy caught it the moment the runner needed that substitution
outside a test. A Protocol cannot express it (contravariant parameters mean
**kwargs promises more than any real client offers), so it is Any with the
reasoning recorded, including what to watch: tests and production drive two
different HTTP libraries.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Rewrite the README against the actual reports

It said "Day 6 of 12" and predated the provenance gate, the filing path and
every extraction number - two days behind the code, on the page a judge reads
first.

Every figure is now read from evals/report.json, evals/cost_sweep.json,
evals/extraction_gemini.json and data/model/win_model.json, and each one was
checked against its source before committing rather than recalled. The
quickstart commands were run verbatim as written.

Structural changes beyond the numbers.

The limitations are now a titled section rather than sentences scattered
through the prose: the LLM drafters have never run live, extraction has
covered 21 of 175 documents, 17 of 20 rulebook entries are unverified, all
data is synthetic, and Razorpay test mode cannot raise a dispute on demand.
A reader who only skims should still hit those, because a judge who finds an
undisclosed limitation themselves discounts everything around it.

The two demos are moved to the top, above the status table. Someone deciding
whether to keep reading should meet the tamper detection and the
disappearing-sentence demo before they meet a checklist.

And there is still no "money recovered" headline. Whether choosing beats
fighting everything depends entirely on an assumed filing cost, so the sweep
is presented as the result and both accountings are shown.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Day 8: the filing path, which is mostly refusals

Stage 7 of 8 had never run. src/vakil/file/ held only the mock, no client
existed, and no test had ever imported either - so the one module that can
change something at a payment provider was completely unexercised. It now
goes end to end against the mock: open -> under_review, documents uploaded,
evidence attached, contest submitted, every step in the ledger.

Four gates stand between a decision and a submission. Verdict must be FIGHT.
Autonomy must be granted - autofile has been computed on every decision since
day 1 and did nothing until now. The deadline must be open. And it must not
already be filed.

That last one reads the ledger rather than memory, because the case that
matters is a retry after a crash and a crash is what destroys in-process
state. The filed marker is written last, after the contest succeeds, so a
crash mid-flight leaves the dispute refileable: a retried filing is
recoverable, a duplicate is not.

Tests drive the real client into the real mock over Starlette's TestClient,
so the mock's own validation runs too - unknown evidence fields, document ids
never uploaded, contests with nothing attached. A hand-written stub would let
client and server each look correct while disagreeing about the wire.

A third undeclared dependency turned up: FastAPI needs python-multipart for
file uploads, so the mock had never been importable, and nothing noticed
because no test had ever imported it. Same shape as the Pillow bug CI found.
The lesson is not "declare dependencies" but that an unexercised module is
not evidence of anything.

Partial evidence still files. A document referenced but missing is skipped,
recorded as document_missing, and the filing proceeds - three of four
documents still argue the case, and refusing over one absent file loses the
dispute outright.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Make an aborted run show the evidence for its own diagnosis

The report said "free-tier quota exhausted" while displaying a body that did
not mention a daily quota anywhere. The classifier reads the full response;
the display truncates at 400 characters, and the per-day metric that triggers
the abort sits past the cut. So a correct classification looked
indistinguishable from the over-broad one D14 had just replaced - the reader
had no way to tell which they were seeing.

The abort now names the marker that decided it: "daily quota exhausted
(matched 'perday')". That confirmed the classification was right and the
allowance genuinely is gone for the day, after 31 requests.

Second gap, found by hitting it: the checkpoint recorded that a field was
wrong but not what it read, so diagnosing one mismatch meant re-sending the
document. On a metered free tier that is the difference between
investigating a failure and deciding you cannot afford to. Wrong fields now
carry read, expected and the source quote, and the report lists every one of
them. Existing checkpoint rows predate the field and simply render nothing,
which is the correct behaviour for a resumable format.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Stop classifying a per-minute rate limit as an exhausted daily quota

D11's classifier matched "exceeded your current quota", which is what Google
returns for both kinds of 429. The resumed extraction run aborted after six
documents claiming the free tier was exhausted; the error carried the detail
that settled it - limit: 5, on a day when 23 requests had already succeeded.
So 5 was never a daily allowance. It is the requests-per-minute ceiling, and
the throttle was set to 10, manufacturing the 429s the classifier then read
as terminal.

The throttle is now 4 RPM, measured rather than guessed. Throttling above a
provider's real limit does not go faster; it converts successes into 429s.

The classifier now requires a per-day metric in the message. Everything else
that returns 429 is a rate limit and gets the retry ladder.

The asymmetry is what D11 got wrong. It framed this as "retrying a wall
wastes hours" and built a detector biased toward calling things terminal.
But a false positive stops a run that would have succeeded, while a false
negative costs one retry ladder. Those are not equal and the detector should
lean toward retrying.

The shape of the mistake is worth more than the mistake: D11 fixed a real
problem and introduced a smaller one pointing the other way, because it was
written while the four-hour failure was still fresh. The guard against
over-correcting is asking which direction of error is cheaper, not which
failure is most recent.

Meanwhile the checkpoint earned its keep on first use - a killed run kept all
7 documents it had finished and the resume skipped them. 13 documents, 65
fields, 100% correct, zero fabrication so far.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Day 7: the provenance gate verifies citations, not prose

The obvious design is post-hoc - let a model write a letter, then check
whether each sentence is supported. That check has to read free prose and
judge whether it seems supported, which is a second model marking the first
one's homework. Two models agreeing is not verification and a reviewer
cannot read either of them.

So the drafter emits structured claims instead. Each sentence names the fact
ids it rests on and the values it states; the gate resolves each citation
against a closed fact index built deterministically from the harvest and
checks the value matches. It resolves or it does not, the same way every
time, in forty lines someone can read.

What that buys, in order of how much it matters:

Withdrawing a document withdraws the sentences that depended on it. `make
draft` against `make draft-without-proof` on the same case drops three
sentences - delivery date, signature, tracking - with nothing invented to
fill the gap.

A real citation carrying a wrong value is the dangerous failure, because it
looks sourced and is false. The asserts field catches it and names the
mismatch.

A factual claim can hide behind a non-factual label, so sentences declared
"argument" are checked for dates, amounts and identifiers. One carrying a
date is a factual claim in disguise and is stripped.

Stripping to nothing is a valid outcome. An empty letter beats a letter of
apologies with the facts quietly removed.

TemplateDrafter is not a placeholder. It runs with no key so CI exercises the
path; it is the baseline a generated letter has to beat on claims verified
and facts used, or the model is decoration; and it is the deadline fallback,
because four hours before a window closes a plain letter that files beats an
elegant one waiting on a rate limit. It cannot hallucinate by construction -
sentences are generated from facts, so an absent fact produces no sentence.
That is a structural guarantee, distinct from the gate's, and the two are
kept separate on purpose.

Both model drafters are written and schema-tested but neither has run live:
the Anthropic account has no credit and extraction exhausted the Gemini free
tier.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Report a tampered ledger as a finding, not a script crash

`make.ps1 verify` exits non-zero when the audit chain has been altered. That
is the tool working - but Invoke-Step treated any non-zero exit as a script
failure and threw, burying the one line that matters under a PowerShell
exception dump:

    TAMPERED record 0 (decide) for disp_...: content altered after write
    verifying audit chain failed (exit 1)
    At D:\Razorpay\vakil\make.ps1:37 char:32
    + ... TEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "$Description failed ...
    ...

Tamper detection is meant to be demonstrated to a panel. The finding has to
be the last thing on screen, not the first line of a stack trace.

Invoke-Step now takes -Verdict, which propagates the exit code without the
throw, so CI and shell pipelines see exactly what they saw before.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Canonicalise the model artefact so it survives a change of platform

CI's staleness guard, once it actually ran, caught a real difference: the
same training data produced a Platt intercept of 0.059706702901627724 on
Windows and 0.05970670290162777 on Linux. 5e-17 - last-bit float64 noise
from a different libm implementation of exp and log. All fifteen
coefficients matched, because those were rounded to six places; the
calibration parameters and the intercept never were.

The fix is a canonical artefact rather than a looser guard. Every persisted
float is rounded to ARTIFACT_PRECISION = 10, which is far finer than any
decision needs - the smallest meaningful move in a probability here is about
1e-3 - and far coarser than platform noise. A test walks the artefact and
asserts no float carries more precision than that, so it cannot regress.

The lesson is about the claim rather than the bug. fit.py has said
"deterministic" since day 6 and it was true as meant: same seed, same
iteration count, no randomness. It was not true in the sense the guard
tests, which is byte-identical output on any machine. Those are different
claims and only the second one supports "CI refits and asserts the artefact
is unchanged". Nothing but a second machine was going to reveal which had
been built.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Fix two broken CI guards, one loud and one silent

The model-staleness guard failed with "fatal: n: no such path". A shell line
continuation had been written as a literal \n, so git was handed "\n" as a
path argument. Loud, obvious, harmless - it never checked anything but it
never pretended to either.

The manifest guard was the real problem. An earlier edit meant to extend it
to data/fixtures/MANIFEST.json silently failed to apply, so for two runs it
passed while checking less than its own name claimed. A guard nobody
verifies is not a guard, and a green check that verifies less than you think
is worse than a red one.

Both rewritten as explicit if-blocks rather than backslash-continued ||
chains. The continuation bought nothing and cost a broken guard.

Underlying cause worth naming: this is the third escaping bug produced by
patching files through Python heredocs - a formfeed in make.ps1, a broken
string literal in extraction_eval.py, and now this. Files containing
backslashes get edited directly from here on.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Declare Pillow, which CI found missing on its first ever run

The fixture generator imports PIL, but pillow was never in pyproject - it
was pip-installed by hand on day 5 and never written down. Every fresh clone
would have failed at `make fixtures`, and nobody would have known until
someone else tried to run the project.

This is the first thing CI caught, on the first run, which is the argument
for having pushed before the code was finished rather than after.

Dev extra rather than a runtime dependency: the generator builds test data,
it is not part of serving a dispute.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Purge two API keys from history and add a pre-commit guard

Two live API keys - one Anthropic, one Gemini - were committed inside
.env.example. Both times the key was pasted into the tracked template rather
than the gitignored .env. The first instance was caught by a manual scan
while staging; the second was not, because that scan never became a standing
check. A repeated failure mode with no guard is a process bug, not bad luck.

Nothing had been pushed, so the history rewrite is clean and complete:
git-filter-repo replaced all three key strings across all 13 commits, and a
scan of the full history now returns zero hits. Had this been found after
the first push, the keys would have been public and unrecoverable.

The guard is a pre-commit hook, enabled via core.hooksPath, matching
Anthropic, Google and Razorpay live-key shapes against staged content only -
so an unstaged edit cannot slip past it. It prints the offending line
truncated and refuses the commit. --no-verify still works, with a note that
this is exactly what someone would say about a real key.

Both keys must be treated as compromised and rotated regardless of the
rewrite, since they were also pasted into a chat transcript.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add a circuit breaker and checkpointing to the extraction runner

A 175-document run estimated at 33 minutes was killed at four hours having
produced nothing. The free-tier daily quota was exhausted and Google holds
each request ~170s before returning 429, so with a per-document retry ladder
of 20/45/90s every document cost about eleven minutes to fail. The first
three failures established the fact; the code proved it another 172 times.

Three fixes, one per mistake.

GeminiUnavailable is now distinct from GeminiError. A malformed document is
worth skipping; a quota or network wall will not improve over the next 174
documents, and the runner stops on it at once. 429 is classified by response
body because the status code alone cannot separate a per-minute rate limit,
which clears on its own and is worth waiting out, from an exhausted daily
quota, which does not.

A circuit breaker aborts after three consecutive failures of any kind. The
counter resets on success so isolated bad pages do not trip it - a breaker
that fires on noise is a breaker people switch off.

Checkpointing appends each scored document to JSONL as it completes, so a
killed run keeps what it finished and a re-run resumes instead of starting
over. Resumed rows count toward the totals, and an aborted run now states
how many documents went unattempted above the metrics, because a partial
run's numbers are a different claim from a complete run's.

Also: granular timeouts, since a bare timeout=120 did not stop a request
that hung, and one reused client instead of one per call.

The estimate itself was the underlying error. "~33 minutes" assumed
throttling was the only per-document cost and that failures would be fast,
both stated as fact rather than as the untested assumptions they were.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Fix the Gemini model id, and make a total failure explain itself

Two bugs, found by the first live run.

gemini-2.5-flash is retired for new keys. The API said so explicitly and
named its replacement, gemini-3.6-flash - my model string was stale. Worth
noting the retry policy behaved correctly here: a 404 is not retried, so ten
documents cost ten calls rather than forty.

The second was worse. When every document failed, the report rendered "No
documents scored" and dropped the errors on the floor, turning a one-line
diagnosis into a hunt through the JSON. A run where everything fails is
exactly when the report has to work hardest. Failures now render in both
paths.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add a Gemini extraction backend so the stage can be measured

The Claude path is verified to the wire - the request reached Anthropic and
came back with a billing error rather than a validation error - but the
account has no credit and buying some was declined. Track 2 asks for
measured results, and an unmeasured stage is worse than one measured on
another vendor's model.

GeminiExtractor sits behind the same Extractor protocol and returns the same
ExtractionResult, so nothing downstream knows which backend ran. Reports are
written per backend rather than to one path, since comparing them is the
point.

Recorded as a funding constraint, not an architectural preference. The system
stays Claude-first and the Claude backend ships either way.

Three things the tests pin, all driven through a mocked transport so no
free-tier quota is spent: the response schema marks every value nullable, so
the model can say it could not read a field instead of being forced to
invent one; a safety-blocked candidate raises rather than reading as a blank
page, which would quietly downgrade real evidence to none; and 429/5xx are
retried with wide spacing while 403 is not, because a bad key will not
improve by waiting.

The schema is hand-written rather than generated from the Pydantic model -
Gemini takes an OpenAPI subset with no $defs or $ref and nullability as a
flag, so a generated schema emits constructs the API rejects.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Day 5: document extraction, scored on fabrication rather than accuracy

Extraction is one of two places a model touches a case, and its output is
deliberately narrow: the model transcribes, it does not decide. It returns
what it read, a verbatim source_quote of where it read it, and an explicit
admission when a field is illegible. Date parsing, address comparison and
every other judgement happen afterwards in ordinary Python. That split is
what makes day 7's provenance gate possible - a claim in the rebuttal can
only survive if it traces to a quote the model said it actually saw.

The eval scores three outcomes, not two. Most extraction benchmarks collapse
"wrong" and "abstained" into "not correct"; that is wrong here. An
abstention costs a missing sentence in a letter. A wrong value puts a
fabricated fact in a document filed with a bank. So the headline metric is
the wrong rate, and a model that abstains more but fabricates less is the
better one for this job. Results break down by document quality, since the
fixtures span clean printouts, scans and phone photographs.

PDFs go to the API directly as base64 document blocks - no OCR pre-pass,
which would flatten exactly the visual context that makes a degraded photo
readable at all.

Default extraction model moved from claude-sonnet-5 to claude-opus-5. The
sonnet default was mine, chosen for cost without being asked; on 175
documents the difference is roughly $3 against $1.20, which is not a reason
to silently pick the weaker model for reading damaged scans. The trade is
now a documented config line rather than a default nobody chose.

A test caught a real ordering bug: the extractor read the PDF before
checking for an API key, so a missing key surfaced as a confusing
FileNotFoundError instead of saying what was wrong.

Live verification is blocked on account credit, not on code - the request
reached Anthropic and returned a billing error rather than a validation
error, which confirms the request shape. The stub backend runs the whole
path with no key and no spend, and is never selected automatically: a
silent fallback would make a broken key look like a working system that
simply found nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Day 6: fit the win model, and find the scoreboard was wrong

Fitted on data/train only, with the calibration method chosen by 5-fold
cross-validation inside the training set. Platt won; isotonic lost, which
is the expected outcome on 200 rows with 8% label noise - it had the
flexibility to carve steps around individual cases and used it.

Held-out: precision 0.436 -> 0.700, F1 0.607 -> 0.789, Brier 0.259 -> 0.175,
and 12 true negatives where there had been none. The engine now folds cases
it believes it would lose. Learned coefficients agree with the domain:
ce3_qualified strongest at +2.15, address_match +1.88, rc_13_3 most negative
at -1.36.

Then the money got worse - uplift versus always-fight fell and the robust
crossover moved from Rs 2,000 to Rs 2,500. Better classification producing
less money usually means the measurement is wrong, so the measurement got
read first.

It was. The EV engine prices Rs 800 of arbitration exposure into every
decision; run_eval.py charged zero for it, on the reasoning that omitting it
was conservative. That held only while the system fought nearly everything.
Once fitting let it fold, the omission became a systematic penalty on
folding: Vakil was declining cases specifically because they carried
arbitration risk, then being scored on a board where that risk was free.

Both accountings are now reported side by side rather than one replacing the
other. Switching to the flattering accounting immediately after seeing it
flatter you is indistinguishable from moving the goalposts, even when the
reasoning is sound; showing the pair lets a reader check it. Charged
consistently, the gap at Rs 250 halves and the robust crossover drops to
Rs 1,200 - inside the plausible manual range rather than at the top of it.
D6's conclusion survives either way.

The escalation margin is now measured rather than chosen: the fitted model's
expected calibration error, 0.089, recorded in the artefact and read by the
pipeline, so refitting moves the abstention threshold automatically. The
chosen 0.08 was within a thousandth of it, which was luck, not method.

The model artefact is committed so evaluation needs no training step, and CI
refits and asserts it has not gone stale - otherwise a corpus change would
leave every reported number describing a model that no longer exists.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Rebuild the venv, run lint and type-check for the first time

The virtualenv's Lib directory vanished mid-session. Rebuilt it with the
full dependency set from pyproject rather than the minimal subset installed
on day 1, which also closes the missing-ruff/mypy gap flagged earlier.

Neither had ever run. CI invokes ruff on every push, so a first push would
have gone straight to a red badge. 14 ruff findings and 19 mypy findings,
all cosmetic - long lines, bare dict annotations, one unused import.

Two judgement calls worth recording. Ruff's B008 fires on every Typer
parameter because the framework declares them as calls in defaults; that is
the required idiom, not the mutable-default bug the rule looks for, so it is
scoped to cli.py rather than worked around. And SIM905 wanted the stopword
list as a 300-character literal; the multi-line set literal satisfies it
without the code getting worse, which is better than a noqa.

mypy now runs in CI too, since it passes clean under strict and a type
checker nobody runs is decoration.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Render proof-of-delivery fixtures, the unscheduled day-5 prerequisite

Corpus cases carry a document_uri pointing at fixtures/pod/NNNN.pdf. Those
were strings with no files behind them, so the extraction stage had nothing
to extract from. Nobody scheduled building them.

175 PODs across three quality tiers - clean carrier printout, flatbed scan,
and phone photograph - because that is the actual distribution in Indian
ecommerce, and an extraction accuracy number quoted without saying which
tier it came from means very little. Ground truth is read from the case
JSON rather than re-authored, so there is one version of the truth and it
cannot drift from the one the oracle used.

The first pass at degradation was far too gentle: the photo tier rendered
almost pristine, which would have made accuracy identical across all three
tiers and the breakdown worthless. Now it applies perspective warp,
single-lamp falloff via multiply blend rather than a wash toward white,
motion blur, contrast collapse and heavy JPEG. Verified by eye - the footer
is near-illegible, which is right.

Pages render at 150 dpi then downsample to 0.97 MP. Claude downsamples above
roughly 1.15 MP anyway, so anything larger costs tokens and buys nothing.
The 25 MB of PDFs are gitignored and regenerable from seed; the manifest
carrying the ground truth is committed, and CI now guards it the same way it
guards the corpus split.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Day 3: cited rulebook and evidence-gap analysis

The plan said "rulebook RAG with citations". Building it hit the obvious
constraint: Visa Core Rules, the VCR dispute-condition guide and the
Mastercard chargeback guide are licensed documents. Scraping fragments into
a public repo is not something a payments company wants to see, and
hard-coding requirements in Python leaves them unciteable.

So data/rulebook/ holds 20 short requirement summaries written for this
project, each citing the rule it summarises, each carrying a verified flag.
Three are verified from Razorpay's public docs; 17 are not, and both
`vakil rules` and the eval report print that count rather than burying it.
A real deployment licenses the rulebooks.

The retrieval decision matters more than the corpus. Reason code to
requirements is a deterministic lookup, not a vector search - the mapping
is twenty rows, and putting approximation between a dispute and the
evidence the network demands is the same category of error as letting the
model pick the verdict. Semantic search exists for the drafting stage's
open-ended questions and filters by reason code rather than boosting,
because citing the wrong dispute condition is worse than citing nothing.
The backend is BM25 in pure Python: no key, no database, and on twenty
short entries not obviously worse than dense retrieval. The pgvector table
stays provisioned and unused behind a Retriever protocol.

Gap analysis maps network requirements onto Razorpay evidence field names -
that bridge is the useful part. Gaps inform the drafting stage and the
console but deliberately do not gate the decision: a human cannot conjure a
missing delivery receipt either, and gating would refill the queue D7 just
drained. Held-out metrics are unchanged, which is correct for a change that
adds information without moving a decision boundary.

One bug worth recording: proof-of-delivery and proof-of-service were both
required for 13.1, but a physical shipment cannot produce a service access
log, so every non-delivery case reported an uncloseable gap. Fixed with
alternative groups. Found by printing output for six real cases before
writing tests - written first, the suite would have encoded the bug.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Move the escalation floor into probability space

D6 left the engine abstaining on 66 of 100 cases at a Rs 2,000 filing cost.
A system that hands two thirds of its inbox to a human has not automated
anything.

The cause was the floor's axis, not its value. Confidence was
|net_ev| / amount against a 0.35 floor, and net EV shrinks as the filing
cost rises, so raising the cost dragged every case toward the floor at
once. The floor was measuring the cost assumption rather than the strength
of the decision. D3 had already moved this once and landed on the same
wrong axis: it expressed doubt in rupees, when the thing in doubt is a
probability.

Everything now collapses into the break-even win probability,
p* = (C + X) / (A + X). The verdict is p_win > p*, confidence is the
distance between them, and a case escalates when that distance is under 8
points - "our estimate would have to be wrong by less than the model's own
error to flip this call". That makes the floor a claim about model error,
which is measurable, so day 6 can set it from observed calibration instead
of choosing it.

Falls out for free: scale-free across dispute sizes, stable under changing
filing costs, and p* > 1 now means the case is priced out entirely and
folds with full confidence rather than deliberating.

Escalation at Rs 2,000 falls 66 -> 34, folds rise 6 -> 14, and D6's
Rs 2,000 robust crossover survives with a larger pessimistic margin
(+Rs 12,000 -> +Rs 16,304). Single-cost precision falls 0.493 -> 0.436,
which is the honest direction - the abstention had been inflating it.

Also surfaces break-even and margin in the CLI, since it is the number that
explains every verdict.

Add cost sensitivity sweep; it narrows what Fight-or-Fold actually claims

Resolves the open question from D5: at the default Rs 250 filing cost the
EV engine almost never folds, so it cannot beat a fight-everything
baseline. Sweeping filing cost from Rs 250 to Rs 2,500 finds the crossover
at Rs 2,000, and splitting by dispute size finds that the small band is the
entire effect - there, fighting everything is outright loss-making.

The first version of the sweep was wrong in a way worth recording. It
credited escalated cases with zero, same as folds, which silently rewards
abstention: raise the filing cost, more cases escalate, and the net
improves because the hard ones leave the accounting. At Rs 2,000 it was
escalating 66 of 100 and being scored on the 34 it kept. Every comparison
now reports both bounds - human folds everything escalated, or fights
everything escalated - and only a win that survives both is marked robust.
The Rs 2,000 crossover does survive.

Consequence: there is no longer a single "money recovered" headline, and
the README says so. Whether choosing beats fighting depends on the filing
cost, which is a parameter rather than a result, so the sweep is the
deliverable. Small-ticket disputes are the product, which is a better fit
for the Indian market than the story we started with.

Default VAKIL_REPRESENTMENT_COST stays at Rs 250 rather than being raised
to make the comparison flatter.

cases on expired deadlines, exposing a date-anchoring bug in the generator
rather than a flaw in the model. See docs/DECISIONS.md D2, D3 and D5 for
